q: An appraisal is best described as:
options: An unbiased, supported opinion of value as of a specific date
A guarantee of the sale price
The listing price set by the seller
wrong: No one can guarantee a price.
The seller sets the list price, not the appraiser.
why: An appraisal is an opinion of value, supported by data, as of an effective date.
hook: Appraisal: an opinion, as of a date, for a purpose.

q: Market value assumes:
options: A typically motivated, informed buyer and seller with no undue pressure
The highest price ever paid nearby
wrong: Distressed sales may not reflect market value.
Related-party sales may not be arm's-length.
Market value is the most probable price, not the highest.
why: Market value is the most probable price in a fair, arm's-length sale.

q: Which federal law requires licensed or certified appraisers for many federally related transactions?
why: FIRREA (1989) set appraiser licensing requirements for federally related transactions.
hook: FIRREA put licensed appraisers on loans.

q: A seller asks a licensee for an "appraisal" to set the list price. The licensee, who isn't an appraiser, should:
options: Offer a CMA and make clear it isn't an appraisal
Prepare an appraisal and sign it
wrong: Licensees can't prepare appraisals without an appraiser credential.
Pricing help is part of the job.
Assessed value often differs from market value.
why: Licensees give CMAs, which must not be represented as appraisals.
hook: Never call a CMA an appraisal.

q: For a mortgage, the appraisal mainly protects:
wrong: The seller isn't the appraisal's client.
Title companies insure title, not value.
why: Lenders need to know the property supports the loan.
hook: The lender wants to know the house covers the loan.

q: Put these appraisal steps in order.
options: Define the problem (purpose, property, effective date)
Reconcile and report the final opinion
why: Appraisers define the assignment, gather data, apply approaches, then reconcile to one value and report it.

q: An appraisal guarantees the price a home will sell for.
wrong: It's an opinion of value, not a guarantee.
why: False.
hook: Appraisal: an opinion, not a promise.

q: USPAP sets standards for how appraisals are developed and reported.
wrong: USPAP is the appraisal profession's standards.
why: True.

q: The appraisal comes in low. Your seller wants you to call the appraiser and insist on a higher number. What should the agent do?
options: Don't pressure the appraiser; if there are relevant comps the appraiser missed, submit them through the lender's reconsideration process
Call the appraiser and demand a higher value
Tell the appraiser you'll never use them again
wrong: Pressuring appraisers violates appraisal independence rules.
Threats to influence value are prohibited.
why: Appraisal independence rules forbid influencing appraisers. Use the lender's formal process.

q: A home's assessed value for property taxes:
options: May differ from its market value
Is set by the listing agent
Is the appraised value for the loan
wrong: Assessments follow tax rules and often lag the market.
why: Assessed value serves taxation and often differs from market value.

q: Highest and best use must be:
options: Legally permitted, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive
The use with the lowest taxes
wrong: The current use may not be the best one.
why: These four tests define highest and best use.

q: An owner spends $70,000 on a pool. In that neighborhood, pools add about $30,000 in value. Which principle explains why value rises only $30,000?
wrong: Conformity is about similarity to the area.
why: An improvement is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost.
hook: Worth what it adds, not what it cost.

q: The largest, most expensive home in a neighborhood of small homes tends to lose value because of:
wrong: Progression is the opposite: a modest home gains among better ones.
Plottage is value from combining parcels.
why: The best home among lesser ones is pulled down: regression.
hook: Biggest house on the block regresses.

q: A new freeway is built behind a neighborhood, and home values drop. This is:
wrong: Nothing about the house wore out.
The owner can't fix an outside cause.
why: Loss from forces outside the property is external (economic) obsolescence.

q: A home has a bedroom you can reach only by walking through another bedroom. This is:
wrong: The cause is inside the property.
That's a valuation principle, not a defect.
why: Outdated or poor design is functional obsolescence.

q: Buyers won't pay more for a home than the cost of an equally desirable alternative. This is the principle of:
wrong: Contribution is about what improvements add.
Regression is about the best home among lesser ones.
why: Substitution underlies the sales comparison approach.
hook: Why pay more for the same thing?

q: External obsolescence is usually incurable by the owner.
wrong: The cause is outside the property and out of the owner's control.
why: True.
hook: Outside causes, out of your hands.

q: Under the principle of conformity, value is highest when a home is similar to the homes around it.
why: True.

q: A worn-out roof is an example of:
why: Wear and tear is physical deterioration.

q: A modest home in a neighborhood of larger, nicer homes tends to benefit in value. This is:
why: Lesser homes among better ones are pulled up: progression.
hook: Smallest house on a great block progresses.

q: Which approach is generally most reliable for valuing a single-family home?
wrong: Best for new or special-use buildings.
why: Homes trade often, so recent comparable sales are the best evidence.
hook: Homes are valued by what similar homes sold for.

q: In the sales comparison approach, adjustments are made to:
wrong: The subject is the fixed point.
why: Comps are adjusted to look like the subject.
hook: Adjust the comp, never the subject.

q: A comparable sold for $412,000 and has a garage worth $15,000. The subject has no garage. What is the comp's adjusted price?
formula: Comp better than subject: adjusted price = comp price − value of difference
steps: The comp has something the subject lacks, so subtract.
why: Subtract the garage's value from the better comp: $397,000.
hook: Comp better, subtract. Comp worse, add.

q: A comparable sold for $375,000. It has two bathrooms; the subject has three. An extra bathroom is worth $12,000. What is the comp's adjusted price?
formula: Comp worse than subject: adjusted price = comp price + value of difference
steps: The comp lacks a bathroom the subject has, so add.
why: Add to the inferior comp: $387,000.
hook: Comp better, subtract. Comp worse, add.

q: Which comparable is most useful?
options: Sold 45 days ago, two blocks away, similar size and age
Sold three years ago, same street
Sold last week, across town in a different school district
wrong: Too old; the market may have changed.
A different location can change value significantly.
A listing is an asking price, not a sale.
why: The best comps are recent, nearby, and similar.

q: Which sale should usually be excluded as a comparable?
options: A sale between a parent and child at a discount
A normal sale through the MLS
A sale two blocks away last month
wrong: Normal market sales are good comps.
why: Non-arm's-length sales don't reflect market value.

q: If a comparable is better than the subject in some feature, the appraiser adds to the comp's price.
wrong: If the comp is better, subtract the feature's value to make it like the subject.
why: False.

q: A comp sold for $450,000. It has a pool worth $20,000 that the subject lacks, but it's 200 sq ft smaller than the subject, at $100 per sq ft. What is the adjusted price?
formula: Adjusted price = comp price − superior features + inferior features
why: The two adjustments cancel out, leaving $450,000.
hook: Comp better, subtract. Comp worse, add.

q: After adjusting several comps, the appraiser arrives at a single value by:
options: Reconciling, giving more weight to the most similar comps
Averaging all of them equally no matter what
why: Reconciliation weighs the comps by how reliable and similar they are.

q: Preparing a CMA, you find two recent nearby sales much lower than your seller hopes. What should the agent do?
options: Include them and explain how they affect the likely price
Leave them out to keep the seller happy
Replace them with older, higher sales
Tell the seller they don't count
wrong: Hiding relevant data misleads your client.
why: Your client deserves an honest picture of the market.

q: The cost approach formula is:
options: Land value + cost of improvements new − depreciation
why: The cost approach values land separately and depreciates the improvements.
hook: Land plus building new, minus wear.

q: Which property is best valued by the cost approach?
wrong: Tract homes have plenty of comparable sales.
Retail centers are valued by income.
why: Special-use properties rarely sell and don't produce rent, so cost is the best evidence.
hook: Rarely sold, rarely rented: use cost.

q: Land is worth $90,000. The building would cost $320,000 to replace new and has $64,000 of total depreciation. What is the value by the cost approach?
hook: Land plus building new, minus wear.

q: The cost to build an exact replica of a historic building, using the same materials, is:
wrong: Replacement uses modern materials for the same usefulness.
Book value is an accounting figure.
why: Reproduction builds an exact replica.

q: A building costs $400,000 new and has a 50-year economic life. Using straight-line depreciation, how much has it depreciated after 12 years?
formula: Annual depreciation = cost ÷ economic life; total = annual × years
why: $8,000 a year for 12 years is $96,000.
hook: Divide by life, multiply by age.

q: In the cost approach, which part is not depreciated?
why: Land doesn't wear out, so it isn't depreciated.

q: Replacement cost uses modern materials to build a structure with the same usefulness.
wrong: That's the definition of replacement cost.
why: True.

q: The cost approach is most reliable for very old homes.
wrong: Estimating depreciation on old buildings is hard, so the cost approach is less reliable for them.
why: False. It's most reliable for new construction.
hook: Cost works best when it's new.

q: A homeowner's insurance policy usually focuses on:
options: The cost to rebuild the structure
wrong: Purchase price includes land and old market conditions.
why: Insurance covers rebuilding the improvements, not the land.
hook: Insure the building; the land survives.

q: A new 2,200 sq ft home costs $185 per square foot to build. What is the construction cost?
formula: Cost = area × cost per square foot
why: 2,200 square feet at $185 is $407,000.

q: A duplex produces $36,000 a year in net operating income. Comparable properties sell at a 7.5% cap rate. What is its value?
A property sold for $1,200,000 and has NOI of $78,000. What is the cap rate, in percent?
A fourplex rents each unit for $1,500 a month. Vacancy and collection loss is 5%, and operating expenses are $21,600 a year. What is the NOI?
formula: NOI = potential gross income − vacancy loss − operating expenses
why: $72,000 less $3,600 vacancy less $21,600 expenses is $46,800.

q: Which is NOT an operating expense when calculating NOI?
why: Debt service isn't an operating expense; NOI measures the property, not the financing.

q: Similar rental homes sell for 150 times their monthly rent. A home rents for $2,100 a month. What's its estimated value?
If NOI stays the same and the cap rate rises, the property's value:
wrong: A higher divisor gives a lower value.
Changing the rate changes the value.
why: Value = NOI ÷ cap rate, so a higher cap rate means a lower value.

q: Which approach is primary for an apartment building?
wrong: Cost is for new or special-use properties.
Comparable sales help, but investors buy income.
Assessed value isn't an appraisal approach.
why: Investors buy income, so the income approach is primary for rentals.

q: A gross income multiplier uses annual income, while a gross rent multiplier usually uses monthly rent.
wrong: GIM is annual for larger properties; GRM is monthly for homes.
why: True.

q: Vacancy and collection loss is added to potential gross income.
wrong: It's subtracted, to reach effective gross income.
why: False.

q: A rental home sold for $288,000 and rented for $1,800 a month. What is its gross rent multiplier?
A comparative market analysis is mainly used to:
options: Help a seller set a list price or a buyer decide on an offer
why: A CMA helps clients make pricing decisions.

q: In a CMA, expired listings mostly tell you:
options: Prices that were likely too high for the market
The exact value of the subject
wrong: No single data point sets exact value.
Low prices tend to sell, not expire.
why: Homes that didn't sell often were overpriced.
hook: Solds show value. Expireds show too high.

q: Active listings in a CMA show:
options: The competition and what sellers are asking
wrong: Only sold prices show what buyers paid.
why: Actives are the competition; they show asking prices, not value.

q: A broker price opinion is:
options: A licensee's estimate of likely selling price, not an appraisal
An appraisal by a certified appraiser
why: BPOs are price estimates by licensees, often for lenders.
hook: Never call a BPO an appraisal.

q: A licensee may label a CMA as an "appraisal" if the comps were carefully chosen.
wrong: Only appraisers prepare appraisals. A CMA must not be called one.
why: False.
hook: Never call a CMA an appraisal.

q: Recently sold comparables are the strongest evidence of value in a CMA.
wrong: Sold prices show what buyers actually paid.
why: True.

q: Your CMA supports about $485,000, but the seller insists on listing at $560,000. What should the agent do?
options: Show the data, explain the risks of overpricing, and document your advice; the seller makes the final decision
Agree to $560,000 and promise it will sell
Refuse to list at any price
wrong: Promising results you can't support is misleading.
You can list it if the seller understands the risks.
why: Give honest advice backed by data, document it, and respect the client's lawful decision.
hook: Advise with data; the seller decides.

q: Three nearby comps sold at $250, $260, and $255 per square foot. The subject is 1,800 sq ft. A reasonable value estimate is about:
wrong: That's too low for $250–$260 per square foot.
That's the price per square foot times 1,000.
hook: Area times price per square foot.

q: Three comps sold for $380,000 (1,900 sq ft), $396,000 (2,000 sq ft), and $361,000 (1,900 sq ft). What is their average price per square foot?
formula: Average = sum of each comp's price ÷ its square feet, divided by number of comps
why: The three comps average $196 per square foot.
hook: Price per square foot, then average.

q: A complete CMA typically includes:
options: Recent sales, active listings, and expired listings
wrong: The seller's old price isn't market evidence.
why: Solds, actives, and expireds together show value, competition, and price ceilings.
